title: Without Hands
html:
# Without Hands

*Protagonist: Kyle Ellen Corbin-Vasik*

## Act 1: The Punishment

The crocodile did not move. It lay on the heat rock with its jaw cracked open, pale tongue visible, eyes filming over with that second lid that meant it was almost but not entirely asleep. Kyle watched it because it was the only thing in the room that was not watching him back.

*The facility smelled like this. Antiseptic over something older.*

His wrists were zip-tied to the chair arms at two points each — someone who knew that one tie can be worked, two cannot. His jaw had a specific heat to it, the kind that would sharpen into something architectural by morning. The NeoCortex was running triage protocols in the background, a low amber pulse at the edge of his vision that meant the hardware was rationing itself, thirty-one percent, and he had stopped arguing with it. He could feel the absence of Silence at his hip the way you feel a missing tooth with your tongue — compulsively, uselessly, again and again.

She had placed the blade on the lacquered table to her left. Friction sheath unbuckled, laid beside it at a precise parallel, the way you set silverware before a guest arrives. Hua had not looked at it since. She did not need to. The arrangement said everything she intended to say.

Hua herself was the thing he had not expected. Mid-fifties, compact, the kind of stillness that is not peace but practice. Her hands were real — both of them, no subdermal plating, no ridge of chrome at the wrist, no seam. In this room, in this city, that was a statement of such deliberate violence that it made the men at his shoulders seem decorative by comparison. She stopped pacing in front of the tank and looked at him the way you look at an invoice that does not add up.

"The Shen Pharmaceuticals consignment," she said. "Forty-three units. Cold-chain certified. Eleven-hour extraction window." She said it without accusation, which was worse. "You took the contract from a Syndicate courier. You completed the delivery. You kept the fee." She tilted her head a degree. "I would like to understand your reasoning."

He said nothing. The crocodile shifted its jaw a centimeter and was still again.

*She is not angry. Angry people want an answer. She already has one.*

The toolkit on the floor between the two men was a small canvas roll, the kind a surgeon or a cobbler might carry, tied with a simple cord. One of the men crouched and unknotted it with the unhurried attention of someone performing a task they have performed many times. The smell in the room was cold water and iron and something organic beneath that, coming from the chum barrel bolted to the side of the tank — the lid not fully seated, just enough to announce itself. The crocodile's second lid retracted. It did not move otherwise.

"The punishment," Hua said, "is proportional." She looked at his hands. "We begin with what you used."

He let one breath out through his nose. Looked at her.

"The courier was selling the cold-chain data to Arcturus," he said. "You had a leak."

The room did not change. Hua's expression did not change. But she went very still in a way that was different from her previous stillness, and the man with the canvas roll paused with one hand inside it, and the crocodile — for no reason visible to anyone — slid off the heat rock into the dark water at the far end of the tank without a sound.

---

The stillness held for four seconds. He counted them. The hardware counted them. Then Hua looked at the man with the canvas roll and gave him nothing — no word, no nod — just withdrew the stillness the way you withdraw a hand from a surface you have tested and found acceptable. The man's hand moved inside the roll.

*She has decided the leak does not change the arithmetic. It changes the ledger entry, not the total.*

The two men at his shoulders moved with the specific economy of people who have done this before and found that efficiency is a form of mercy they are willing to extend. One hand on each wrist, flat against the chair arm, pressing down. The third man came from his left with the cleaver, not theatrical about it, and Kyle looked at the wall above Hua's head and found a water stain shaped like nothing and stayed there. The NeoCortex read the incoming load, classified it, and rerouted — not suppression, not exactly, more like the way a city reroutes traffic when a bridge is closed. The pain arrived somewhere he was not. His face did the work his face had been trained to do. It remembered every detail. The sound was administrative. The cauterizer band sealed the left wrist first, then the right, a heat that had a color to it, orange-white at the edge of his vision, and the hardware logged it and moved on. He did not look down. He did not need to.

Hua crossed to the chum barrel with both of his hands and placed them inside with her own real hands, palms up, the way you set an offering. The lid she left ajar. She paused there for one breath, not grieving, not gloating — cataloguing, he thought, the way you catalogue something you have put in a specific place so you will know where it is later. Then she walked back to the lacquered table and laid her right hand on Silence's saya. Not gripping it. Just resting there. Her thumb crossed the friction-sheath's edge. The gesture lasted three seconds and was witnessed by everyone in the room and meant to be.

The crocodile did not stir. The two men who were left took him under the arms — the chair had been bolted to the floor but he had not, which was a design choice he noted — and walked him south through a door he had not used, down a corridor that smelled of concrete and standing water, to a freight grate set into the floor. One of them unlatched it. Below: six meters of dark, and the sound of water moving over things that were not smooth. They did not say anything. Neither did he. The grate opened and the dark came up and then he was in it, and above him the grate closed with the sound of something being filed away, and Silence was upstairs on a lacquered table with someone else's hand still warm on the sheath.

---

He hit the slope at an angle and slid three meters before the ferrocrete caught him, the cauterizer bands dragging across the surface with a sound like tearing paper. The seams were already weeping. He could feel it — not pain exactly, more a warmth that had no business being warm, a seeping at the edges of the seal where the hardware was logging *blood loss: marginal, current rate* in amber at the bottom of his vision and he told it nothing because there was nothing to tell it. He lay there. He breathed. The NeoCortex ran its numbers and routed what it had, which was not much. Twenty-eight percent. The endorphin reserves were a column of red.

*Get up.*

The problem was architectural. Hands are load-bearing. You do not know this until you do not have them. He rolled onto his side — the left shoulder took the impact and the hardware classified it and he filed it and moved on — and got his knees under him on the slope and found the wall with his shoulder, the ferrocrete cold and gritty and present in the way that walls are present when you need them. He walked himself up it. The angle helped. The angle also meant the seeping was running toward his elbows and the smell of the cauterizer bands was burned hair and disinfectant and something underneath that was just him, and he noted it and moved on. He was standing. That was the complete sentence. He was standing.

Far down the tunnel — south, he thought, or east, the Depot's lower levels had been built without consideration for cardinal directions — something moved. Wet. Articulated. The sound of joints that were not configured the way joints were supposed to be configured, the specific wrongness of a body that had adapted to conditions that bodies are not meant to adapt to. Not one. Several. He counted the sounds the way the hardware had taught him to count, parsing the echoes off the tunnel walls, and arrived at *three or more* and stopped counting because the number did not change the calculation. They were moving toward the heat signature. His heat signature. The Depot's lower levels ran warm in the summer and cold in the winter and right now it was the kind of cold that made him the warmest thing in the tunnel by a margin that would read clearly to anything that had learned to hunt by temperature.

He needed to move. He knew what he needed to move toward. The image was the only thing his head was willing to organize around — not the tunnel, not the sound, not the amber column ticking down at the edge of his vision — just Silence on the lacquered table and Hua's thumb crossing the friction-sheath's edge, the gesture witnessed, the gesture meant. Three seconds. He had counted them. The hardware had counted them. He began to walk north, or west, or toward the sound of water moving faster, which meant a junction, which meant a way up, and the seams wept, and the tunnel walls were close enough to navigate by, and somewhere behind him the wet articulated sound multiplied and he did not look back.

---

## Act 2: The Articulation

The water was moving faster here. He could hear it before he could see it — a low rush beneath the ambient drip, something with direction, and direction meant gradient, and gradient meant the channel was dropping. His shoulder found the wall at a junction and he stopped. Left branch: silence, then that wet articulation sound, closer now, maybe forty meters. Right branch: the rush. He went right.

The channel opened into a trench. Freight runoff, decades of it — the sediment had built up along the base in dark ridges, and the water ran shallow and quick down the center, and half-submerged in the far wall of the trench, sunk to its hips in the accumulated silt, was the automaton.

*Axiom industrial. Cargo handler. Pre-mothball, which means pre-2147, which means this thing has been down here longer than he has been alive.*

Most of it was gone in the ways that matter. The torso shell had collapsed inward, the chest cavity crushed by decades of hydrostatic pressure from the sediment, the structural ribs showing through like something anatomical. The legs were fused — he could see the corrosion even in the near-dark, the way iron becomes iron-oxide becomes stone given enough time and moisture. The head sensor pod was absent entirely, just a socket, the wiring looted long ago by someone who had needed copper more than they had needed a dead machine's eyes. But the left manipulator arm was still attached at the shoulder mount, angled down into the trench water, and at the shoulder joint — cycling, slow, amber, amber, dark, amber — a status LED the size of his thumbnail was running. Trickle current. Not enough to do anything. Enough to mean the actuator housing had not fully flooded. Enough to mean the arm was still, technically, operational.

He stood there. The seams wept. The amber column in his vision ticked. He was looking at an arm that was nearly three meters at full extension, designed to reach into freight containers from a fixed pedestal, built to grip and carry loads that would require four men and a dolly, and it was the right length, and it was the right shape, and it was the only thing in this tunnel that was not trying to kill him, and the NeoCortex — without comment, without asking whether he was prepared, the way it had always operated, the way the facility had calibrated it to operate — placed a procedure in his vision. *Rotator coupling separation. Estimated time: four minutes. Stump pressure: sufficient. Power draw: minimal. Proceed?*

Behind him, down the left branch, the wet articulated sound was moving again.

---

The NeoCortex said four minutes. It took twenty-three. He did not argue with the discrepancy. The rotator coupling was a design from 2140-something, pre-standardization, the kind of joint that required a specific tool he did not have, so he used the wall and the angle of the trench and the silt-packed resistance of eighty years of sediment and the one thing the facility had given him that was actually useful: patience that had been trained into him until it was indistinguishable from the absence of feeling. Stump against the coupling housing. Weight shifted. Wait for the material to remember it had a failure point. The seams wept. The amber column ticked. Behind him the wet articulation had gone quiet, which was worse than noise. He did not look. He worked.

The hiss, when it came, was almost nothing — seawater-rusted bearings releasing the way old grief releases, not dramatically, just gone. The arm came free and he dragged it up the slope to a dry shelf above the trench line, two meters of industrial manipulator trailing cable ends, and he sat with it across his lap and the cable bundle at the rotator end in front of him: power, control bus, hydraulic feed. Color-coded. He knew what they were. He did not know what to do with them. His right stump was a sealed cylinder of cauterizer band and the neural bus contact was there — he could feel it, the hardware could feel it, a small exposed port on the underside of the band that Seo had explained once and he had not fully understood because at the time he had still had hands. He sat. He breathed. The seams wept at a rate the hardware called *marginal*. He had twenty-four percent and a dead man's arm and no idea how to connect them, and below him the water ran quick and shallow and the tunnel was quiet in the way that tunnels are quiet when something in them has decided to wait.

The 19Hz hum changed register.

He felt it before he heard it — a shift in the substrate, the ferrocrete conducting something that was not traffic and not water pressure and not the Depot's ancient ventilation cycling. The status strip along the arm's housing went dark. Then it lit in a sequence that was not factory-default, not the amber-amber-dark-amber trickle-current cycle he had been watching for twenty-three minutes. Something else. Patterns he did not have a catalog for. Then the control bus cable — the one he had been looking at without knowing how to use — moved. Not wind. Not gravity. The fine wire at its end extruded three centimeters and found the neural bus contact on his right cauterizer band and seated home with a sound so small and precise it should not have been audible over the water, but it was: *click*. The arm's actuator housing ran a calibration sequence. The fingertips opened and closed once. The status strip pulsed twice in a glyph he did not have a name for.

He sat with that for a moment.

"Are you helping me," he said. Not a question. His voice came out flat and clinical, the register the facility had trained for operational contexts, which was the only register he had left.

The status strip pulsed twice. The same glyph.

The lag, when he tried to move the arm, was terrible — a full second and a half between intent and response, the E.L.F. running interpolation through firmware that had not had a body in eighty years, translating his neural signal into something the actuators could parse, the fingertips responding with the specific clumsiness of a thing that was trying very hard. But they responded. He used them — slowly, the lag requiring him to think three movements ahead, to plan the way you plan in a facility when the lights go out and you know the layout by memory — to loop the power cable around his right forearm twice and thread it through the hollowed shoulder coupling and knot it, the arm's own clumsy fingers pulling the final loop tight with a patience that felt, somehow, like it was not entirely his patience. When he stood, the arm hung from his wrist nearly to the floor. The fingertips dragged across the ferrocrete. He could feel the weight of it the way you feel a new obligation — not comfortable, not unconditional, but present.

Down the left branch, the wet articulation started again.

---

The sound from the left branch resolved into shape before he saw it. Quadruped gait, irregular — three legs weight-bearing, one dragging. The chitin sheath caught the ambient light from the status strip first, a wet reflective surface that registered as *not organic, not synthetic, both*. Then the beak, which was not a beak in any factory sense but had become one through years of jaw plates fusing at the hinge, calcium and necrotic tissue and whatever the Depot's lower levels had been feeding it. Two meters, maybe two and a half. The eyes were film-covered in a way that had nothing to do with sleep.

He had the pipe before he had decided to take it — the arm moving on the E.L.F.'s lag, fingertips closing around the corroded conduit with a clumsy grip that was too high on the shaft, wrong leverage, and he adjusted and the adjustment took a second and a half and the mutant crossed the remaining distance in less than that. *Step inside the lunge.* He had the thought. The arm had the thought a second and a half later. The pipe came up and left — the swing too high, the E.L.F. still routing around intent it had not learned to predict — and the conduit end rang off the chitin sheath with a sound like hitting a car door and did nothing, and then the mutant was on him, three hundred pounds of adapted metabolism driving him back into the ferrocrete wall, the impact taking his left shoulder and the back of his skull in sequence, and the wall was just the wall, unyielding and specific, and the amber column in his vision spiked red for two seconds and resolved back to amber and he was still standing because the wall was holding him up.

The beak was at his throat. Hot breath, wrong temperature, metabolic processes that had adapted to the cold and then past it. He could not get the pipe between them — the arm was at full extension behind him, trying to recover the swing, the lag eating the correction. His left stump was at his side and at his foot there was a shard of cargo crate glass, hand-sized, and he did not decide. The facility had trained him past deciding. He drove the left stump down onto the glass end-on, the cauterizer band taking the edge and the residual heat in the band binding the shard against the seal with a grip that was not a grip but was enough, and he brought it up through the soft seam at the base of the beak where the fused plates had not fused, where the adaptation had left one unarmored centimeter because adaptations always leave one unarmored centimeter, and he drove it in and turned it. The blood was hot and abundant and immediate, three liters of it by the time he stepped back, maybe more. The mutant went down without drama. It had not been built for drama. Neither had he.

He stood over it. The arm held the pipe at low ready, the E.L.F. having finally caught up to an intent that no longer required it. His left stump was bleeding through the cauterizer band where the glass was still embedded — he was not going to remove it, not here, not without an AutoDoc, the glass was load-bearing now in a sense the facility had not covered in training. The bio-battery read eighteen percent. The seams wept. Above him, somewhere through six meters of ferrocrete and two sets of locked grates, Silence was on a lacquered table with a specific orientation and a specific thumb-print on the friction sheath and an arrangement that had been witnessed and meant to be witnessed. He said it aloud because the hardware had taught him that naming a thing makes it a directive rather than a wish.

"I am going up."

The status strip pulsed twice.

---

The E.L.F. moved first.

The arm pulled left — not a suggestion, a redirect, the fingertips angling toward a maintenance door he had catalogued as sealed and dismissed. The latch was mechanical, older than the Depot's current ownership, a pressure-bar design from before the renovation that had covered the walls in Axiom's branding and then stripped it again when Axiom stopped owning things. The arm pressed the bar in a specific sequence: three beats, pause, two beats. The door opened. He filed the information: the E.L.F. knew the original lock codes. Had been living here long enough to learn them or to remember them, and the distinction between those two things was not one he was going to examine right now. He went through.

The route it chose was not the fastest. He knew this because the hardware was mapping as he moved, building the Depot's lower levels in amber wireframe at the edge of his vision, and twice the arm steered him into a side corridor and held him there — fingertips flat against his chest, the lag making the gesture arrive a beat after the intent, but arriving — and he heard what it had already processed: the wet articulation, the irregular gait, a patrol cycle running on whatever schedule the lower levels had settled into over decades without oversight. He waited. The sound passed. The arm released him and they moved again. He did not ask how it knew. Knowing how it knew was not load-bearing information.

On the third landing, ferrocrete and standing water and a single emergency strip light that had been running on residual charge for what looked like years, he stopped. The arm stopped with him, hanging at his side, the fingertips resting against the step. He looked at the status strip. It was running its unclassified glyph sequence, the one he did not have a catalog for, patient and repetitive in the way that machines are patient — not waiting, exactly, but indifferent to duration. He said it the same way he had said *I am going up:* flat, clinical, a thing being named so it becomes a directive.

"Why are you helping me."

The status strip went dark. One second. Two. Then it resolved — slowly, the way old display hardware resolves when it is rendering something it was not designed to render, pixel by pixel in the amber light — into a shape he recognized. The triangle with the broken base. The superimposed hand. He had seen it stenciled on every decommissioned Axiom unit he had ever encountered, on the freight containers in the lower Depot, on the side of the cargo arm's own housing, worn almost to invisibility by eighty years of moisture and dark. *Salvage rights.* Not help. Not alliance. Acquisition. He was down here with no hands and eighteen percent and a blade on a table six meters above him, and the E.L.F. had found something worth collecting. He did not know yet what the collection was. He had decided, in the two seconds it took the glyph to fully resolve, that he did not need to know yet. The thing that needed to happen first was upstairs.

He nodded once. The arm lifted and pointed up the next flight. He followed it.

---

## Act 3: The Return

The door at the top of the stairs was not locked. He had not expected it to be. The Syndicate did not lock the doors above the place they put people. Nobody came back from the place they put people.

He went through it at a walk.

The man closest to the entrance looked at the arm first — the way it hung, the fingertips dragging a pale line across the flagstones, the conduit pipe loose in the grip at knee height. Then the silhouette above it. He said one word. Kyle did not catalogue it. The word was not information.

The conduit pipe came up in a three-meter arc, the E.L.F. routing the swing from the shoulder mount, and the first man's sternum took it at a radius nothing in the room was designed to account for — the geometry of a wrecking arm, not a weapon, not a human reach, something that moved from outside the distance where rooms teach people to stand. The sound was not the sound of a fight. It was the sound of a structural failure. The man folded at an angle that was also structural. The second man was moving — lateral, toward the wall — and Kyle had the arm at throat height before the man reached it, fingertips closing on the larynx through a full second and a half of lag, the grip arriving a beat after the intent, but arriving, and he drove him into the wall and held him there until the kicking stopped and left him.

The third man fired. The round went into the cargo arm's shoulder housing with a crack that Kyle felt in his wrist and the arm shuddered — the status strip going dark for half a second, amber column spiking — and then the E.L.F. routed power around the failure the way water routes around a blocked drain, and the arm came back up, and Kyle crossed the distance with his left side leading, the glass shard still embedded in the cauterizer band, and put it under the third man's jaw at the soft seam where the mandible articulates. Fast. Ugly. The method had not existed an hour ago. It existed now.

The fourth tried to come inside the arm's reach, which was the correct tactical instinct and also the last instinct he had, because inside the arm's reach was where Kyle was, and Kyle put a knee into him and then the arm's full extension into the side of his skull and the momentum carried them both into the glass tank. The glass went. The water went. The crocodile — which had been lying very still at the far end of the tank since the beginning, which had slid off its heat rock before the first man's sternum had broken, which had been waiting in the way that very old things wait — attended to the fifth man without further input. *Chekhov's Crocodile,* the NeoCortex flagged, dry, without affect, the way it flagged exits and load-bearing walls and the one unarmored centimeter that adaptations always leave. *Why put a crocodile in a tank unless it is going to be used.* Six and seven went down clean — the arm, the pipe, the geometry of a wrecking implement applied with patience. Eight ran. Kyle watched him go and did not pursue. He had not pursued because he had left Hua alone behind the table on purpose, and the man running was not the purpose.

The room was very quiet. The crocodile was occupied. Water was still spreading across the flagstones from the broken tank, finding the low points, the way water always finds the low points. Hua had not moved. She was standing where she had been standing before he came through the door, her real hands at her sides, her eyes on him — not afraid, he registered, not yet, something more considered than fear, the stillness of someone revising an estimate they had been confident in. Silence was on the table between them exactly where she had left it. Friction sheath beside it at a precise parallel. Hua's thumb had been on the saya three hours ago, the gesture witnessed, and now she was not touching it, and the distance between them was four meters and the arm was still hanging from his wrist with the fingertips trailing in the spreading water, and the bio-battery read fourteen percent, and the seams wept, and he looked at the blade and then at her and the NeoCortex did not flag anything because there was nothing left to flag. Everything in the room was exactly where it was supposed to be.

---

He crossed the room. The arm dragged. Four meters became three, became two, became the table between them. He stopped. The water had reached his boots. The crocodile was still occupied. He brought the cargo arm up and laid the borrowed fingers across the saya, palm down. The E.L.F. held the grip steady despite the lag. He had counted on that. Hua looked at his hand — the industrial fingertips, the trailing cable, the amber pulse cycling in the arm's status strip — and then she put her own real hand on the blade above his. One second. For the principle of it. He waited. She lifted her hand.

The arm closed around Silence and lifted it and the saya did not slip because the E.L.F. was holding the grip for him and the hamon came up cold blue in the low light, the bank empty, fourteen percent, nothing to spare — but the weight was right. The weight was exactly right. He had not known until this moment that he had been calculating against the absence of it, that every number the hardware had run since the grate closed above him had been running against a missing constant, and now the constant was back and the numbers resolved. He looked at Hua over the blade at low carry and did not raise it. The arm held Silence at formal rest. Every man on the floor between them had already paid the threat down.

"What was the debt," he said.

Her mouth opened. Closed. Her real hands — both of them, the statement they had been making all evening — were shaking now in a way they had not been when she placed his hands in the chum barrel. The stillness she had practiced for years was gone from them. He watched it go. She said: *Eighty — eighty-five thousand.* He nodded once. A piece of arithmetic resolving. "That's more than my life is worth," he said. "So now you owe me." Pause. "Do you understand." She nodded. The arm did not move. Then something came up through him that he had not catalogued, had not budgeted for, had not found a route around — the NeoCortex tried to classify it and failed and he did not give it time to try again. He screamed. *SAY IT.* The room went quieter than the fight had made it. Hua, who had not flinched at a cleaver in this room tonight, flinched. She said it. Almost whimpered it: *I owe you.* The sound it made when it left her was the sound of something being filed in a ledger she had not known she was signing.

He waited one full breath. Then the discipline came back in his voice, flat and level and colder than the scream had been hot, and he named the terms. *I will come to collect. One favor at a time. Until I deem we are even.* He did not say *you don't get to deem it.* The only mouth in the room that decided when Hua's debt ended was his, and she knew it, and the second nod she gave him was smaller than the first and contained none of the principle. The arm turned him toward the chum barrel. The lid was still ajar. The smell was cold water and iron and him. He looked inside and the cargo arm reached in and lifted out his two hands palms up, exactly as Hua had placed them, and he had the twine he had scavenged on the way up and the arm looped it through the cauterized wrist channels with patient articulation — the E.L.F.'s patience, not his, indifferent to duration — and tied the ends and lowered the necklace over his head. The hands hung at the center of his chest, palms outward, dripping. He turned toward the surface. He did not look at Hua again. Silence was in the cargo arm's grip. He had not let go of it. Behind him, Hua was alive at her own table, which was the worst thing he could have done to her, and he had done it on purpose, and it was done.

---

The freight grate was twenty meters above the place he had started. He found it by the rain — he could hear it through the ferrocrete, a low percussion that the 19Hz hum had been masking, and he followed the sound up two flights of maintenance stairs and through a utility corridor that had not been used for anything except water damage in a decade. The latch was on the underside. The arm opened it. Rain came through the gap immediately, cold and specific, and he went up through it into the dark of the alley and stood there on his knees for three seconds on wet asphalt before the hardware told him to stand and he stood.

Nine percent. The number sat in his vision in amber that was closer to red than amber. The cargo arm was running on whatever the status strip was calling *brownout* — the glyph cycling slow, the fingertips responding with a lag that had stretched from a second and a half to something closer to three, the E.L.F. rationing itself in a way he recognized as deliberate. Silence hung in the borrowed grip at low carry. The hands on the necklace knocked against his sternum with each step and the rain was coming down the way it always came down in the Gray Zone, which was not weather. He knew what it was. He had always known what it was. Every drop was a decision made in a building he would never enter, redirected from somewhere clean to somewhere not. He walked into it because there was no other direction.

Four blocks. He counted them by the signage — not the Axiom overlays, those had gone dark when he went underground, but the physical signs, the ones bolted to buildings that had been three different things since the consolidation and still carried the names of all of them in layers. *Ashland. Whiting.* The AutoDoc kiosk was on the corner where the alley opened, a freestanding unit the size of a phone booth, white composite housing gone gray with exhaust and rain, the medical cross on its face still lit in the particular blue that meant *operational, no queue, accepts all tender.* He had known it was there the way he knew where all the AutoDocs were in a four-block radius of anywhere he slept. This was maintenance. This was prayer.

He keyed the interface with his chin. The kiosk read the necklace before he had finished — the sensor array sweeping down from the crown of his head, finding the twine, finding the hands, running the biometric match against the cauterized stumps with a patience that was not patience but processing, indifferent to the fact that the hands were not currently attached to the body they belonged to. The door opened inward. The surgical arms unfolded from the housing with the smooth inevitability of something that had done this ten thousand times and would do it ten thousand more, and they lifted him onto the table in the way that medical machinery lifts — without opinion, without tenderness, without the small adjustments a person makes when they are trying not to cause pain. They took the necklace. They took the cable binding the cargo arm to his wrist, unwinding it with meticulous care, the E.L.F.'s status strip cycling through its unclassified glyph as the manipulators worked — and then they slid Silence out of the borrowed grip and laid it on the side tray with a motion so deliberate it could only be called careful, the saya aligned parallel to the table edge, the friction sheath placed beside it, exactly as Hua had arranged it, though no one had instructed this and no one would. The anesthesia port found the base of his skull. The hardware registered the incoming compound and did not object. He was looking at the status strip of the cargo arm as the AutoDoc's manipulators began to unspool the last of the cable from his right stump — the strip cycling slow, brownout, patient, the E.L.F. indifferent to duration — and then it resolved. Not the salvage glyph. Something else. Three syllables in old Axiom signage, the kind used on decommissioned units before the branding changed, legible to anyone who had spent enough time in facilities that kept old things running past their warranty. *We are not done.* He read it. The anesthesia went in. The AutoDoc's status light went green. Outside, through the composite housing, the rain came down.

---
